newsitem.title: USA: Friends, neighbors heap praise on McVeigh.
newsitem.headline: Friends, neighbors heap praise on McVeigh.

text.p: A jury weighing a death sentence for convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh heard him praised on Monday as a cheerful youth, an excellent student and a model soldier who saved a man's life on the battlefield.
Defence attorneys trying to persuade the jury to spare McVeigh's life called a succession of former neighbours and Army colleagues who gave glowing testimonials for McVeigh.
Capt. Jesus Angel Rodriguez, McVeigh's commanding officer during the Gulf War, testified that McVeigh gave first aid to another soldier who was hit by shrapnel and "basically saved his life."

The jury of seven men and five women that found McVeigh guilty last week of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people in the worst mass murder in U.S. history, is weighing whether he should be sentenced to death or to life imprisonment. The prosecution wants a death sentence.
The defence, which has called 21 witnesses in the penalty phase so far, resumes its case on Tuesday. The case is expected to go to the jury later this week.
Rodriguez said that when he had to return to the United States because his brother-in-law had been killed in an accident, McVeigh was "really compassionate. He showed that he really cared," he said.
"Sgt. McVeigh was an outstanding soldier. He did what he was told, anticipated what had to be done (and) took pride in his work," Rodriguez said.

McVeigh, 29, expressionless through much of his trial, looked more lively on Monday. He smiled often when his former friends and neighbours brought up memories, such as an anecdote by Rodriguez about his fondness for strawberry pop tarts.

Deborah Carballo, one of McVeigh's former teachers at a high school in Lockport, New York, said McVeigh was an excellent student with above average intelligence who never had any disciplinary problems. "I remember him as among the best students," she said.
McVeigh smiled and shook his head as if embarrassed when defence attorneys introduced his class yearbook, which said McVeigh had been voted "most talkative" by his classmates.

Lynn Drzyzga, a former neighbour of the McVeigh family in Pendleton, New York, said McVeigh was about nine years old when he began playing with her children. "I just enjoyed having him around," she said.

McVeigh used to run around barefoot so Drzyzga made him wear a pair of socks when he came into her house to avoid dirtying the furniture. Years later, when McVeigh visited, he had a pair of socks on his shoulder. "That was special," she said.

Fighting back tears, Drzyzga told how McVeigh visited the family shortly before going to the Gulf War and told of his foreboding he would not return alive. "He said: 'Mrs. D. I'm coming home in a body bag.' I said: 'You must get those thoughts out of your mind.'," she testified.

"Tears welled up in his eyes and he hugged me and he walked away very slowly," she said. "It was like my own son was leaving." Drzyzga said she put a yellow ribbon on the maple tree in their garden for McVeigh, only taking it down when he returned home safely.

Drzyzga's husband, Richard, said that as a boy, McVeigh was "a great kid, funny, always cheerful." But he said he was scared when McVeigh sent him a videotape critical of the government after the 1993 federal siege at Waco, Texas.
The government says McVeigh blew up the Murrah building to avenge the deaths of 80 Branch Davidians at Waco.
The Drzyzgas sent McVeigh a letter, enclosing a picture of their son who was about to join the Air Force.

Richard Drzyga testified that McVeigh returned the photograph, bent, with a note saying: "Do you ever wonder why there are yellow fringes on the flag?" Some extreme right-wingers believe a fringe around the flag has military connotations.
Also in the letter, received six months after Waco, was a videotape about Waco that Drzyzga and his wife watched.
"It made an impression on me, it scared me," Drzyzga said. He said he asked his wife: "What the Hell's he gotten into?"

Drzyzga said he was torn and confused in his feelings about McVeigh. "There's a part of me that still remembers Timothy McVeigh as a little kid. Then there's a part that sees what everybody else sees on television and gets angry and I can't put the two together," he said.
